---
title: "2. Rare and emerging markers: k13 R622I"
description: >
  Mapping a marker that most surveys never find: the artemisinin
  partial-resistance mutation k13 R622I, emerging in Eritrea and Ethiopia.
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 110,
                      out.width = "100%")
library(ggplot2)
```

The kelch13 R622I mutation confers artemisinin partial resistance. It has
emerged in the Horn of Africa, notably in Eritrea and Ethiopia, and is one
of the markers national programmes in the region now track. A marker like
this differs from crt K76T in [tutorial 1](crt76t.html) in three ways:

- **most surveys find nothing**, so the data are mostly zeros;
- **the signal is local and recent**: a few areas, in the last decade;
- **the questions are about thresholds**: where is prevalence probably
  above a level that matters for policy?

This tutorial uses the same frame and workflow as tutorial 1, and dwells on
what changes.

```{r packages}
library(stareal)
```

## 1. The data, and why the zeros matter

```{r stave}
url <- paste0("https://github.com/IDEELResearch/scrub/raw/2d85d021efe1c93dc55300610d944c9fbaf4af1a/",
              "analysis/data-out/stave_data_2026.03.17.rds")
tmp <- tempfile(fileext = ".rds")
download.file(url, tmp, mode = "wb", quiet = TRUE)
stave <- suppressWarnings(readRDS(tmp))
igad <- c("Djibouti", "Eritrea", "Ethiopia", "Kenya", "Somalia", "South Sudan", "Sudan", "Uganda")
```

STAVE stores the variants each study reported. A survey that genotyped
codon 622 and found only the wild type records `k13:622:R`, not a zero for
`k13:622:I`. So the raw counts for the exact string `"k13:622:I"` contain
only the surveys where the mutation was found:

```{r counts-vs-prevalence}
counts <- merge(stave$get_counts(), stave$get_surveys(), by = c("study_id", "survey_id"))
counts <- counts[counts$variant_string == "k13:622:I" & counts$country_name %in% igad, ]
c(surveys = nrow(counts), with_positives = sum(counts$variant_num > 0))

p <- stave$get_prevalence("k13:622:I")
p <- p[p$country_name %in% igad & p$denominator > 0, ]
c(surveys = nrow(p), with_positives = sum(p$numerator > 0))
```

`get_prevalence()` finds every survey that genotyped the codon: 423, of
which 400 found no R622I. A model fitted to the 23 positive surveys alone
would map a marker present everywhere it was looked for. The 423 surveys are
the package's `igad_k13_622i`:

```{r data-table}
all.equal(sort(p$survey_id), sort(igad_k13_622i$survey_id))
surveys <- igad_k13_622i
agg <- aggregate(cbind(positive, tested) ~ country, surveys, sum)
agg$prevalence <- round(agg$positive / agg$tested, 3)
agg
```

## 2. Frame, time and cells

The frame of tutorial 1, and years from 1994, the first survey:

```{r frame-data}
fr <- areal_frame(igad_adm1, id = "id", groups = c(country = "country"),
                  link_within = "country", adjacency_snap = 2000, verbose = FALSE)
tf <- time_frame(1994, 2024, "year")
d <- areal_data(surveys, fr, tf, y = "positive", k = "tested",
                coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), date = "collection_day")
d
```

```{r data-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(d)
```

## 3. Fitting

```{r load, include = FALSE}
cache <- readRDS("_cache/k13-622i.rds")
fit <- cache$fit
fit$data$frame <- fr              # the cache stores the fit without its frame
```

A pilot with the defaults first, as in tutorial 1:

```{r pilot, eval = FALSE}
pilot <- fit_areal(d)
diagnose(pilot)
```

```{r pilot-checks, echo = FALSE}
cache$pilot_checks
```

This time the pilot fails. Mostly-zero data say little about each cell, so
the chains move slowly through the latent values and the hyperparameters.
The remedy is a longer run, with the same call as for any marker:

```{r fit, eval = FALSE}
fit <- fit_areal(d, control = list(n_iter = 20000, n_burn = 5000, n_store = 250, theta_thin = 10),
                 checkpoint_dir = "chains/k13-622i")
```

```{r diagnose}
cache$checks
summary(fit)
```

```{r traces, fig.height = 5}
plot(fit)
```

The longer run passes every check. Compared with crt K76T:

- `sigma` is about 4, against 2.5. The field has to carry prevalence from
  near zero across most of the region to 10% or more in a few units, a range
  of several units on the logit scale.
- The intercept, about −5 on the logit scale (under 1%), is the regional
  baseline. The interval of the trend spans zero widely: one linear trend
  for the whole region cannot describe an emergence confined to a few areas,
  so the field carries it instead.
- `rho_s` and `rho_t` are close to 1: the model spreads a local signal
  smoothly to neighbouring units, and lets it persist from year to year.

## 4. Where has R622I emerged?

```{r predict}
pr <- predict(fit, groups = "country", exceedance = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1), verbose = FALSE)
```

Country trends:

```{r countries, fig.height = 5}
plot(pr, group = "country", ids = c("Eritrea", "Ethiopia", "Somalia", "Sudan", "Kenya", "Uganda"))
```

```{r country-table}
subset(pr$groups$country, time %in% c("2015", "2020", "2024") & id %in% c("Eritrea", "Ethiopia", "Djibouti"),
       select = c(id, time, mean, q50, q2.5, q97.5, p_gt_0.05))
```

Maps of the posterior mean, and of the probability that prevalence exceeds
5%:

```{r maps, fig.height = 4}
m <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("2015", "2020"), function(y) sf::st_as_sf(pr, time = y)))
g1 <- ggplot(m) + geom_sf(aes(fill = mean), colour = NA) + facet_wrap(~time) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("R622I\nprevalence") + theme_void()
g2 <- ggplot(m) + geom_sf(aes(fill = p_gt_0.05), colour = NA) + facet_wrap(~time) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c("P(prevalence\n> 5%)", limits = c(0, 1), option = "magma") + theme_void()
patchwork::wrap_plots(g1, g2, ncol = 1)
```

In 2015 no unit is more likely than not to exceed 5%; by 2020 seven are.
Which units, and what data stand behind each?

```{r hotspots}
hot <- subset(pr$area, time == "2020" & p_gt_0.05 > 0.5)
hot$name <- igad_adm1$name[match(hot$id, igad_adm1$id)]
hot$tested <- tapply(pr$area$k, pr$area$id, sum)[hot$id]     # over all years
hot$positive <- tapply(pr$area$y, pr$area$id, sum)[hot$id]
hot[, c("name", "country", "mean", "q2.5", "q97.5", "p_gt_0.05", "tested", "positive")]
```

The table says three different things:

- **Gash-Barka (Eritrea) and Amhara (Ethiopia) have the data**: hundreds
  tested and dozens positive. Most of the R622I in the data was found
  there; Tigray, Afar and Debub add a few more.
- **Maekel (Eritrea) has no surveys of codon 622 at all.** Its probability
  comes from its neighbours, among them Gash-Barka and Debub.
- **Galgaduud (Somalia) rests on one parasite**: one tested, one positive.
  Its interval runs from 0.1% to 94%. One sample with the mutation is a
  reason to look, not a finding.

Djibouti makes the same point at the scale of a country. It has no surveys
of codon 622, yet its 2020 mean (`r round(100 * subset(pr$groups$country, id == "Djibouti" & time == "2020")$mean)`%)
is higher than Eritrea's. Its posterior is wide and skewed: Eritrea and
northern Ethiopia are next door, and the data cannot rule out that R622I is
there too. The mean is pulled up by that tail, well above the median.

With a rare marker, the map of the mean shows where the model cannot rule
the marker out as much as where it is. Read it with the map of the data
(section 2), the intervals, and the exceedance probabilities.

## 5. What the model assumes, and when to doubt the map

- **One variance for the whole region.** The field is stationary: the same
  `sigma`, `rho_s` and `rho_t` in every area and year. An emergence is a
  local, growing departure, and the model accommodates it by inflating
  `sigma`. The inflated variance then applies everywhere, which is why
  unsurveyed areas (Djibouti, most of Somalia) have such wide intervals.
- **After the last survey, the median falls back.** The latest surveys of
  codon 622 in Eritrea are from 2019, and in Ethiopia from 2021. Beyond
  them, the AR1 process decays toward the regional baseline, so the 2024
  medians are lower than in 2020 and the intervals wider. A stationary
  model cannot extrapolate a spread. The 2024 map says the data stop, not
  that R622I receded.
- **Where the surveys were made.** Studies of an emerging marker are often
  sited where resistance is suspected, for example after treatment
  failures. The model assumes that survey locations tell it nothing about
  prevalence. If studies chase the mutation, the surveyed units overstate
  their neighbours.
- **A zero is worth its sample size.** 0 of 50 is not unusual when
  prevalence is 5%: it happens `r round(100 * dbinom(0, 50, 0.05))`% of the time. The
  binomial likelihood weighs each zero by its denominator, but many small
  zeros do not prove absence.

Covariates that track the process, such as drug pressure or transmission
intensity, can take over part of what the field does here.
